correctness.rationale: For positive a,b the tensor Hamiltonian has four explicit orthogonal projectors, and the only possible eigenvalue collision occurs at am=bn. The bright/dark decomposition is established by finite-dimensional semigroup spectral arguments, not simulation. Summing the four distinct projectors gives the off-resonance efficiencies; at collision merging exactly two projectors gives a nonnegative square divided by positive weights and the exact listed resonance deficits. All dimensions including m=2 or n=2 and any positive absorber strength are covered. The independently built full labeled-Hamiltonian Krylov projectors passed 246 exact checks and independent non-Hermitian dynamics passed 32 checks; finite tests corroborate but are not substitutes for the proof.

originality.rationale: Scope-narrowed claim is the all-size anisotropic single-trap law on rectangular K_m square K_n, m!=n, with a unique resonance a/b=n/m and strictly positive losses in each of three nontrap source classes. Direct primary full-text inspection identified Razzoli et al. (2021) Eq. (25), which already implies the isotropic square case: that case is explicitly excluded from the novelty claim and used solely as a known comparison. Rectangular graphs fail strong regularity, and examined general dark-subspace methods do not explicitly state their two-parameter piecewise table; targeted published-record searches and comparison with related earlier research claims yielded no equivalent statement. This is evidence-qualified same-model originality, not a uniqueness certificate. Historical-priority uncertainty persists.

value.rationale: The rectangular Cartesian product of two complete interaction communities is a natural exactly solvable quantum-network family, not a numerical slice. Unequal sides yield two inequivalent neighbor classes and a distinct nonneighbor class. The theorem identifies the unique tunable anisotropic collision ratio and closed losses at all sites, including a strictly positive nonneighbor defect for every rectangle; the previously known isotropic square case has zero such defect. This contrast is a meaningful geometry-induced boundary benchmark for near-dark transport and for understanding why tiny coupling detuning changes eventual capture. It does not claim a downstream theorem or finite-time singularity.
